title: Testing a working niche and sharpening it with client response
audience: Owners in any service business who have shortlisted a focus and need a method for deciding between candidates.
learningOutcomes: Write a working niche statement that is marked as provisional and has a review date
Answer the ten decision questions for the two strongest candidates and record the answers
Use prospect response and an affordability check to decide whether to keep, refine or replace the niche

instruction.heading: Settling on a focus takes time
instruction.body: Many people find it hard to settle on one focus, and the decision can take months. Treat your first niche statement as a working niche: a provisional choice you intend to test, review and possibly change. Writing it down, with a review date you can keep, makes the decision concrete without locking you in. Being unsure is normal. What matters is that the decision is tested against evidence on a schedule, rather than left open indefinitely.

instruction.heading: Test the working niche by offering it
instruction.body: The quickest way to sharpen a niche is to describe it to real people and see what happens. Speak with about ten prospects in the group, offer the service in its working form, and record what you hear: questions asked, objections raised, quotes accepted, and enquiries that went no further. Silence is information too. Make each approach relevant and honest, and do not pressure anyone: the ACCC's 2026 media release on unsolicited selling reports that many approaches were pressured or misleading. The response is the feedback that tells you whether to keep the niche, refine its wording or replace it.

instruction.heading: Ten questions to narrow the choice
instruction.body: When two or three candidates remain, answer ten questions for each. Which clients have you enjoyed working with most? Which clients come to you without much effort? What work gives you the most energy? When in the working day do you feel most at ease? How do you want your days to look in this business? Which option has the strongest buying triggers for its group? Which option is most commercially sensible? Which is easiest to deliver well? Is anyone else serving this group successfully? Their success is evidence that demand exists, though it is not a reason to copy them. Would you rather commit now and aim for profit sooner, or keep your options open for longer? Write each answer in full. A candidate with strong triggers but weak personal fit will show up clearly.

instruction.heading: Check whether the group can afford you
instruction.body: A niche only works if the group can pay the price the business needs. Not every decision is about money, but choosing a group that cannot afford the work is not a sound plan. Compare the price you need with what the group can reasonably spend, using the test in “Defining target segments from customer data” of need, ability to pay and reachability. Before quoting anyone, confirm their budget, timing and deadline, and check your own capacity; Business Queensland advises this. If the gap is large, you have three options: change the group, change the offer or price, or keep looking. A change to price must rest on evidence and on your costs, not on hope.

instruction.heading: Decide at the review date
instruction.body: On the review date, look at the response log, the answers to the ten questions and the affordability check. Then choose one of three outcomes: keep the working niche and write its final statement; refine the wording, the group or the offer, and test again; or replace it with the next candidate. Record the outcome and the reason. Stopping to reconsider is a legitimate business decision, not a failure.

procedure: Write the working niche statement and a review date you can keep
Contact about ten prospects in the group and offer the working form of the service
Record every question, objection, quote and silence in one response log
Answer the ten decision questions for the two strongest candidates
Run the affordability check against the price the business needs
On the review date, choose to keep, refine or replace, and record the reason

workedExamples.situation: A solar panel cleaner has tested two groups over several weeks: homeowners with rooftop systems, and strata committees. Home enquiries are frequent but small. Strata enquiries are fewer but larger, and some committees have asked for a written scope.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which niche should she keep as the working niche, and what should she record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The strata candidate is the stronger working niche, because the response shows larger jobs and clear requests. She records the enquiry counts, the scope requests and her answers to the ten questions for both groups. She checks affordability by comparing the committees' likely spend with the price she needs, and sets the next review date. Working-at-height and safety requirements are outside this lesson. Check the work health and safety rules for your state or territory before taking on that work.

workedExamples.situation: A landscaper is torn between steep-block gardens and garden upkeep for rental property turnover. Both candidates scored well on the fit factors, but only the rental candidate has produced repeat work.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which candidate should she test next, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: Repeat work is evidence the rental candidate can hold a client, so it should be kept as the working niche. She can still test steep-block gardens with one pilot job at full price, recording the response, and compare the two at the review date.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
A prospect response log with dates and outcomes
The ten decision questions, answered in writing for each candidate
The price and cost figures from the business plan

commonErrors.error: Treating the first niche as permanent, and never testing it
commonErrors.prevention: Write a review date when the niche is declared, and keep it.

commonErrors.error: Changing the niche after one weak week
commonErrors.prevention: Collect about ten prospect responses before deciding.

commonErrors.error: Using the decision questions to find reasons to avoid a niche you fear
commonErrors.prevention: Answer the questions honestly for every candidate, including the one you hoped to avoid.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Advertising a working niche to test it must meet Australian Consumer Law obligations on claims and pricing. The ACCC's page on misleading claims covers accurate claims and misleading price offers; check the wider law before relying on this point.
Follow-up messages to prospects sent by email or text can be commercial messages under the Spam Act, which requires consent and a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days.
Licence notice: where the niche involves licensed work, this lesson does not grant or confirm any licence. Licence rules are set by each state and territory, so check with the relevant regulator.

qualityStandard: A working niche statement has a recorded review date
The response log holds at least ten prospect contacts before a decision is made
The affordability check records the price used
The review outcome (keep, refine or replace) is recorded with its reason
documentationEvidence: Working niche statement with its date and review date
Answers to the ten decision questions for each candidate
Affordability check and the review decision record
summary: A niche is a working decision, declared provisionally and tested on a set date
Prospect response, including silence, is the evidence that sharpens a niche
Answer the ten questions for the strongest candidates before deciding
Check that the group can pay the price the business needs, then keep, refine or replace

knowledgeChecks.question: What does calling a niche a 'working niche' mean?
options: It is provisional, tested with real prospects, and reviewed on a set date
It cannot be changed once it has been declared and it must stay the same for years
It is copied from the most successful competitor in the area

knowledgeChecks.question: Prospect responses are weak for the working niche. What is the best use of that result?
options: Keep the niche for a year, since weak early responses are normal
Treat it as evidence to refine or replace the niche at the review date
Lower every price in the business to match the group

knowledgeChecks.question: Which check belongs with the choice of a niche?
options: Whether the niche is the most popular topic on social media
Whether the niche has a logo in the business colours
Whether the group can afford the service at the price the business needs

knowledgeChecks.question: How many candidates does the lesson say to answer the ten decision questions for?

officialReferences.title: False or misleading claims (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission)
officialReferences.pageDate: no date in page body; page metadata shows published and modified 28 June 2026
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (WebFetch). Says claims about price, product, value and delivery must be accurate, and that a business must be able to prove any claim it advertises. Covers misleading price claims, including conditional 'free' offers and sale prices that were never real. Does not address testing an offer before the full price applies. Publisher: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

officialReferences.title: Email and SMS unsubscribe rules (Australian Communications and Media Authority fact sheet)
officialReferences.covers: Read (ACMA fact sheet, Email and SMS unsubscribe rules). Supports that commercial messages must generally include an unsubscribe, opt-out or stop option; that requests must be actioned within 5 working days; that the opt-out must be free; and that it must work for at least 30 days after the message is sent without requiring an account, login or extra personal information. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).
